Anglesey: Wales' Island Gem for Motorcyclists

Anglesey — Ynys Môn in Welsh — is Wales' largest island and a destination that consistently surprises visiting riders. Connected to the mainland by Telford's magnificent Menai Suspension Bridge and the Britannia Bridge, this 276-square-mile island packs in a remarkable diversity of landscapes. Dramatic sea cliffs, tranquil beaches, ancient Neolithic sites, and a 125-mile coastal path encircling the entire island make Anglesey far more than a transit stop on the way to the Holyhead ferry.

The Coastal Circuit

The single best ride on Anglesey is the coastal circuit — roughly 75 miles following the coast road around the entire island. Starting from the Menai Bridge, head clockwise via Beaumaris, Red Wharf Bay, Amlwch, Cemaes Bay, Holyhead, and back through Newborough. The roads are well-surfaced, traffic is light outside Holyhead, and the sea views are constant. Allow a full day with stops.

Key Destinations

  • Beaumaris — Stunning medieval castle (UNESCO World Heritage Site), elegant Georgian buildings, and excellent restaurants on the Menai Strait
  • South Stack Lighthouse — Dramatic lighthouse on a tiny island off Holyhead, reached by descending 400 steps down the cliff. RSPB reserve with thousands of seabirds
  • Red Wharf Bay — Vast tidal bay with excellent seafood at the Ship Inn, one of Wales' most scenic pubs
  • Newborough Warren and Llanddwyn Island — Forest, dunes, and a tidal island with lighthouse ruins and views of Snowdonia
  • Amlwch — Former copper mining port, now a characterful harbour village on the north coast

Ancient Anglesey

Anglesey has been inhabited for at least 8,000 years and is extraordinarily rich in prehistoric sites. Bryn Celli Ddu is a 5,000-year-old passage tomb aligned with the summer solstice. Barclodiad y Gawres is another Neolithic tomb with rare carved stones. Din Lligwy is a well-preserved 4th-century settlement. The island was the last stronghold of the Druids before the Roman invasion of AD 60 — Tacitus recorded the terrifying scene of Druid priests cursing the Roman legions across the Menai Strait.

Anglesey is the kind of place where you stop to photograph a beach and end up standing inside a 5,000-year-old tomb. The island layers its history so casually that you stumble across millennia at every turn.

Food and Local Character

Anglesey has strong food credentials. Halen Môn sea salt is exported worldwide and used by top restaurants. Local seafood — particularly lobster, crab, and Menai Strait mussels — is superb. The Oyster Catcher at Rhosneigr and the Lobster Pot at Church Bay are outstanding seafood restaurants. Beaumaris has several excellent dining options. The island is also home to Anglesey Sea Zoo and the Foel Farm Park.

Views of Snowdonia

One of Anglesey's unexpected pleasures is the view back to the mainland. From the southern and eastern coasts, the full panorama of Snowdonia rises dramatically across the Menai Strait — Snowdon, the Glyderau, and the Carneddau create a mountain wall that's particularly spectacular at sunset or after fresh snow.

Practical Information

Anglesey is accessed via the A55 expressway from Chester (90 minutes) or Bangor (10 minutes). Both the Menai Suspension Bridge and Britannia Bridge carry traffic to the island. Fuel is available in Holyhead, Llangefni, Benllech, and Menai Bridge. Accommodation includes hotels in Beaumaris and Holyhead, B&Bs throughout, and several excellent campsites. The island is compact enough to explore in a full day, but a weekend allows proper exploration. Best months: May to September. Winds can be strong on exposed coasts — check conditions before riding the Holyhead Mountain area. The island hosts the Anglesey Circuit motorsport track at Ty Croes if you fancy a track day.

The island is extraordinarily rich in prehistoric sites, including the 5,000-year-old Bryn Celli Ddu passage tomb.

faq.q: Can I do a track day on Anglesey?
faq.a: Yes. The island hosts the Anglesey Circuit motorsport track at Ty Croes, one of the most scenically located circuits in Britain with the Coastal layout running along the Irish Sea. It is popular for track days, so if you fancy some circuit time it makes a memorable addition to a touring trip to the island.
